title: Coordination Compounds
seo_title: Coordination Compounds Class 12 Chemistry Worksheet with Answers (NCERT Chapter 5)
standard_text: Coordination compounds – introduction, ligands, coordination number, colour, magnetic properties and shapes, IUPAC nomenclature of mononuclear coordination compounds. Bonding, Werner's theory, VBT and CFT; structure and stereoisomerism, importance of coordination compounds (in qualitative analysis, extraction of metals and biological system).
meta_desc: Free CBSE Class 12 Chemistry worksheets for NCERT Chapter 5 Coordination Compounds: Werner's theory, ligands and denticity, coordination number, oxidation state, IUPAC names, isomerism, VBT and crystal field theory. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: The complex ion is written in square brackets.
key_sub: Coordination number = number of donor atoms bound to the metal.
body_html:
How to think about it

In a coordination compound a central metal ion is bound to ligands that each donate electron pairs. The coordination number counts the donor atoms: [Co(en)₃]³⁺ has 6 because en is bidentate. Werner showed that only ions outside the square brackets are free, so [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ gives 3 ions and 2 mol of AgCl.

IUPAC names list ligands alphabetically before the metal and its oxidation state, with -ate for anions. Complexes show geometrical, optical, linkage and ionisation isomerism. Crystal field theory splits d orbitals into t₂g and eg; strong field ligands such as CN⁻ give low-spin complexes.

Example

[Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃: ions?

1 + 3

Answer: 4

Example

Oxidation state of Fe in [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻?

x − 6 = −3

Answer: +3

Common mistakes

  • Counting chloride inside the brackets as free.
  • Counting en as one donor atom.
  • Forgetting -ate for anionic complexes.

items.q: How many ligands surround the metal ion in [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>?
items.e: [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> has 4 Cl ligands, each forming 1 co-ordinate bond (co-ordination number 4).
